title: Geoeconomic coercion can target foreign governments, private firms, or both
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35343; theoretical model of great-power geoeconomic coercion through trade and financial linkages
geography: United States/China-style hegemonic relationships with foreign governments and private firms

observations.period: Model framework; trade and financial-linkage coercion scenarios

denominator.unit: theoretical model entities and equilibrium scenarios; no observed-country or event denominator

target_entities.value: foreign governments and foreign private firms

private_target_advantage.value: private entities internalize less than their government the equilibrium consequences of acquiescing

government_target_advantage.value: a targeted government can potentially influence domestic firms that the hegemon has limited direct power to coerce

optimal_target_mix.value: depends on the relative strength of private-target and government-influence channels

observed_compliance.unit: firm response, government response, public cost, alliance behavior, and strategic outcome

observations.method: Theoretical geoeconomic model in which great powers use existing trade and financial linkages to pressure foreign private entities and governments; the model compares the incentive and influence channels for each target type.
observations.uncertainty: The model identifies mechanisms and optimal-target conditions, not empirical frequencies or success rates. It does not estimate a particular sanction, export-control, investment-screening, or coercion episode.
observations.subgroup: Modeled foreign governments and private firms in countries connected to a hegemonic power through trade and finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Private targeting may reduce national internalization of the consequence but can impose concentrated firm costs; government targeting may reach more firms but may also provoke resistance or coalition formation. The model does not determine which occurs in a real case.

related_sources.claim: Carbon-tariff policy is a separate climate-trade model and is not pooled with the target-selection theory.

boundary: This record adds a model-based target-selection mechanism for geoeconomic coercion. It does not establish which target type is used more often, whether a target complies, who bears the cost, how domestic publics respond, whether alliances change, or whether coercion achieves a strategic objective.
